items.title: Air France Flight 447
items.summary: The aircraft entered a stall after unreliable airspeed indications during cruise and impacted the Atlantic Ocean.
items.probableCause: The investigation examined pitot-probe icing, loss of reliable airspeed information, flight-control inputs, stall recognition and crew response as part of the accident sequence.

items.title: Asiana Airlines Flight 214
items.summary: During approach to San Francisco International Airport, the aircraft struck the seawall short of the runway and was destroyed by impact and post-crash fire.
items.probableCause: The investigation focused on approach-energy management, automation understanding, monitoring, crew coordination and fatigue-related performance factors.

items.title: United Airlines Flight 232
items.summary: A catastrophic failure of the tail-mounted engine led to loss of all three hydraulic systems; the crew attempted an emergency landing using asymmetric thrust.
items.probableCause: The NTSB traced the initiating engine failure to an undetected fatigue crack associated with a metallurgical defect and shortcomings in inspection and quality-control processes.

items.title: TWA Flight 800
items.location: Atlantic Ocean near East Moriches, New York, USA
items.summary: The aircraft broke up in flight shortly after departure from New York following an explosion in the center wing fuel tank.
items.probableCause: The NTSB concluded that the center wing fuel-tank fuel/air mixture ignited; the exact ignition source was not determined with certainty.

items.title: Qantas Flight 32
items.summary: An uncontained engine rotor failure caused significant structural and systems damage shortly after departure from Singapore; the crew returned and landed safely.
items.probableCause: The investigation found a fatigue crack in a non-conforming oil-feed pipe that released oil, led to an internal fire and ultimately to turbine-disc failure and debris release.

items.title: British Airways Flight 38
items.summary: The aircraft lost thrust on both engines during final approach and landed short of the runway.
items.probableCause: The investigation identified restricted fuel flow associated with ice accumulation in the fuel system under the specific operating conditions.

items.title: Emirates Flight 521
items.summary: The aircraft impacted the runway during an attempted go-around and was destroyed by post-impact fire; all occupants evacuated, while one firefighter was killed.
items.probableCause: The investigation examined go-around initiation, thrust-command logic, crew actions and energy state during the rejected landing sequence.

items.title: Lion Air Flight 610
items.summary: The aircraft crashed shortly after departure following repeated nose-down stabilizer commands associated with erroneous angle-of-attack data.
items.probableCause: The final report identified interacting design, certification, maintenance and crew-response factors in the accident sequence.

items.title: Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302
items.summary: The aircraft crashed shortly after takeoff following erroneous angle-of-attack information and repeated automatic stabilizer commands.
items.probableCause: The investigation focused on flight-control design behavior, sensor input, crew workload, procedures and certification assumptions.

items.title: US Airways Flight 1549
items.summary: Following a multiple bird strike and loss of thrust in both engines, the crew ditched the aircraft in the Hudson River.
items.probableCause: The NTSB identified bird ingestion into both engines and the resulting near-total loss of thrust as the initiating event, with survivability aided by crew response and evacuation.

items.title: Indonesia AirAsia Flight 8501
items.summary: The aircraft entered an upset and prolonged stall during cruise after a sequence involving recurrent system faults and crew actions.
items.probableCause: The investigation linked recurring rudder-travel-limiter system faults, maintenance history and subsequent crew handling to the accident sequence.

items.title: Germanwings Flight 9525
items.summary: The aircraft was deliberately flown into terrain during cruise descent.
items.probableCause: The investigation addressed deliberate pilot action as well as aeromedical oversight, confidentiality and risk-detection issues.

items.title: American Airlines Flight 587
items.summary: The vertical stabilizer separated after large alternating rudder inputs following wake turbulence shortly after takeoff.
items.probableCause: The investigation focused on excessive rudder pedal inputs, rudder-system characteristics, training and structural loads on the vertical stabilizer attachment.

items.title: Alaska Airlines Flight 261
items.summary: The aircraft lost pitch control after failure of the horizontal stabilizer trim-system jackscrew assembly.
items.probableCause: The NTSB identified insufficient lubrication and maintenance-program issues that led to excessive wear and failure of the stabilizer trim mechanism.

items.title: Japan Airlines Flight 123
items.summary: A structural failure of the aft pressure bulkhead led to explosive decompression, major empennage damage and loss of hydraulic control.
items.probableCause: The investigation traced the failure to an improperly executed repair of the aft pressure bulkhead following an earlier tail-strike event.

items.title: China Airlines Flight 611
items.summary: The aircraft broke up in flight after long-term fatigue cracking propagated from an earlier structural repair area.
items.probableCause: The investigation identified an inadequate repair following a previous tail strike, allowing fatigue cracking to grow over many years.

items.title: Turkish Airlines Flight 1951
items.summary: The aircraft stalled on final approach after an erroneous radio-altimeter signal affected autothrottle behavior and the developing low-energy state was not corrected in time.
items.probableCause: The investigation examined radio-altimeter malfunction, automation response, crew monitoring and approach-energy management.

items.title: Southwest Airlines Flight 1380
items.summary: A fan blade separated in flight, causing an uncontained engine failure and fuselage-window damage followed by rapid depressurization.
items.probableCause: The investigation identified a low-cycle fatigue crack in a fan blade and examined inspection-method effectiveness and containment behavior.

items.title: Atlas Air Flight 3591
items.summary: The cargo aircraft entered a rapid descent and impacted a bay while on approach to Houston.
items.probableCause: The investigation focused on inadvertent go-around-mode activation, spatial disorientation, crew performance and training/selection issues.

items.title: UPS Airlines Flight 6
items.summary: An in-flight cargo fire led to severe smoke, system degradation and loss of control during the attempted return to Dubai.
items.probableCause: The investigation examined lithium-battery fire hazards, cargo-fire detection/suppression limitations, smoke penetration and system degradation.

items.title: United Airlines Flight 811
items.summary: A forward cargo door opened in flight, causing explosive decompression and major fuselage damage.
items.probableCause: The investigation examined cargo-door electrical/mechanical locking design and the ability of the door to appear latched without all locking sectors fully engaged.

items.title: American Airlines Flight 191
items.summary: The left engine and pylon separated during takeoff, damaging systems and leading to asymmetric stall and loss of control.
items.probableCause: The investigation identified maintenance-induced structural damage in the pylon attachment sequence as a critical initiating factor.

items.title: Qantas Flight 72
items.summary: The aircraft experienced two uncommanded pitch-down events in cruise, causing passenger and crew injuries before a diversion and safe landing.
items.probableCause: The investigation examined erroneous air-data/inertial reference inputs and flight-control computer response to invalid angle-of-attack data.
